maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair there is a matter I should like to lay before the house. This matter affects over two thousand men engaged in the fishing industry on the Fraser river. For the information of the house I might say that on February 10, 1933, an order in council was passed by the present government at a time when the house was in session. This order in council permitted seine boats to operate in the mouth of the Fraser river. I protested against this order in council as did the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), but in spite of our protests it was put into effect in the fall of 1033. I rise today to air the grievances of over two thousand fishermen on the Fraser river who are affected by this order in council. The order in council changed the boundaries which had hitherto precluded seine boats from operating in the mouth of the Fraser river and permitted them to go in and fish in that area. I also wrote to the minister last fall in connection with this matter and perhaps if I read my letter it would explain the whole situation very fully. This letter was dated September 23, 1933, and reads:	.
The Hon. Alfred Duranleau,
Acting Minister of Fisheries,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. Duranleau:
I am writing you in connection with the matter of allowing seine boats to operate at the mouth of the Fraser river, which action, done by order in council, you will remember, was opposed by me at the time on the floor of the house.
The chief argument advanced by you and also by the deputy minister of fisheries was that it was desirable to use seines in order that only the best salmon be procured for canning purposes, so as to enable the canners to put up the best grade possible in order to enable them to compete with other countries on world markets, particularly the market in Great Britain.
As you will know, I was particularly interested in the effect of this drastic regulation, and what the effect would be on the individual gill net fishermen. I have made further investigations into this, and believe it might be of interest for you to know what has actually happened by allowing seine boats to operate right outside the mouth of the Fraser river.
I understand over 60 seine boats have been operating in the new area, and to the positive detriment of individual gill net fishermen. In fact, if seine boats are going to be allowed to operate permanently, then thousands of men
are going to be thrown out of employment and the government might as well face this serious responsibility right now.
In other years, and before the seiners were permitted there, the daily catch of individual fishermen ran all the way from 100 to 800 pinks, or humpbacks per day's operations. This year the seiners have scooped them up by the thousands with this result, the catch of the gill netters has dropped from 800 to next to nothing. Some seine boats scooped up eight or nine thousand pinks in one day's operations, whilst fishermen from the mouth of the river up, were only catching from 20 to 60, and in some instances only 10, and when you consider the low price offered, namely 3 cents for male, and 1 to 2 cents for each female humpback, you will realize just how serious the outlook is for the fishermen depending on this for a livelihood on the river.
I informed the house during the time of the debate that gill netters could operate in the area where seiners are now allowed to fish. In support of this, I will quote you one day's operations in the gulf of Georgia.
On the 19th of September, 80 gill netters landed 1,985 pink salmon, an average of 24 fish each, w'hilst 7 seine boats operating there landed between 7,000 and 8,000 pinks, an average of over 1,000 each seine boat. Both gill netters and seiners were paid the same price, the fish caught being of equal quality, so that j'ou will have to advance some other argument other than that of better fish coming from the seine boats.
It may be that seine boats operating far out in the gulf, and in clear sea water, catch pinks that have a somewhat better colour, but I would again draw your attention to the fact, that the area where seine boats have been operating at the entrance to the Fraser river, the waters there being brackish and muddy with silt. You must go a considerable distance out before the line of demarcation commences, and the point where the clear sea waters meet the fresh muddy waters of the Fraser river is plain to be seen by the naked eye, but let me again repeat, the new area allotted to seining is all brackish waters.
To sum up, hundreds of fishermen are being deprived of their legitimate livelihood and many will be forced on relief. I maintain this is a terrible state of affairs, and very bewildering indeed. Here is the government endeavouring on the one hand to give employment to the unemployed and the destitute, whilst on the other hand we have a department of the government helping to create by its own actions, more unemployment.
I again appeal to you to rescind the order in council for if it is not done, and further seining is allowed to continue, all individual gill net fishermen will be thrown out of employment, and in closing, I ask you to note carefully that according to the new regulations laid down, whilst the seiners are allowed to catch this year pinks of humpbacks, next year it will be the sockeye salmon.
I remain,
Yours respectfully,
I received an answer dated September 29, which reads as follows:
I am much obliged for your letter of the 23rd instant, with regard to purse-seining
Salmon Fishery:-Mr. Reid

operations in the lower portion of the gulf of Georgia, which were permitted this year for pink salmon.
The operations in this area have been carefully followed. The outcome was not far different from what was anticipated.
You urge that the quality of fish taken by the seiners was no better than that of the fish caught by the gill-netters, so that the regulation is not resulting in a better quality product, but, if persisted in, will have the effect of throwing thousands of men out of employment.
My information is that there were times when sets were by some of the seiners in the shallow water over the mud flats when the tide was high and that the fish caught in these nets were no better than those taken by the gill-netters, but that these catches totalled a very small portion of the fish caught. The one fact that for most of the fish taken by the seiners prices as high as seven, eight and nine cents were paid, while the catches of the gill-netters brought only four cents at the same time, and some as low as three, speaks for itself. While final figures are not before me, the information available indicates that between 75,000 and
100,000	cases of good pinks will have been put up this year in the Fraser river district, as a result of this regulation. Two years ago, when the last big run was on, and when there was no seining allowed, nor was the inspection of canned salmon in operation, only 21,534 cases of these fish were put up in the Fraser area. While the fish were passing through United States waters 705,580 cases were put up. This year the pack on the United States side was approximately 465,000 cases.
You are surely overlooking some facts regarding employment when you say that if this regulation operates permanently thousands of men are going to be thrown out of employment. As a matter of fact, up to the end of October of last year there were 760 white gill-net fishermen on the Fraser. These had twenty-four assistants, making 784 in all. I have not yet the figures for this year, but they would not likely be very different. Also, the pink fishery is by no means the main factor in the Fraser river gill-net fishermen's operations. On the other hand, the employment given the seiners must not be entirely overlooked'. On the sixty boats that operated in the district this year there would likely be an average of eight men each and these would all be whites.
As you will know, the time the pinks remain in the area south of the Fraser, after they have reached it. before they make for th* Fraser depends on weather conditions. This year m.v information is that the runs did not start until the 13th instant and shortly afterwards the pinks began to ascend the Fraser in large numbers, then reasonable catches could be made by the gill-netters. The regulation in no way prevented earlier fishing by the gill-netters, the fact being the fish were not in their area at that time. The inevitable happened when the fish struck the fresh water. Their quality rapidly deteriorated so that they no longer would' make a good quality pack and it obviously is in the best permanent interests of the salmon fishery of British Columbia as a whole, and consequently of the fishermen engagfMr. Reid.]
ing in it, that the quality of our pack should
be assured.
While the seining operations were very carefully patrolled this year, it may be that in the light of experience some additional marking of the seining area will be desirable. The whole matter will be gone into carefully.
I wish to point out some inaccuracies that occur in this letter in reply to mine. No doubt the minister received the information from his deputy or from the department; nevertheless I maintain that there are in that letter some inaccuracies of which he may not be aware. He mentions, I will not exactly say cunningly, but he mentions that there were 760 white gill netters. That is not the exact number and I wonder why he did not mention the whole of the gill net licences issued and in operation on the Fraser river, because my information is that some 1,707 gill net fishing licences had been issued for operation on the river, and that there was also a total of 348 boat pullers, making altogether 2,055 who were affected by this regulation. The minister says that the regulation in no way prevented fishing by gill netters, and) he states the fact that the fish were not in this area at that time. Well, how could the gill netters or anyone else catch fish there if the fish were not there? That is not a sound argument, because there were times when the fish were in that neighbourhood. He speaks of the fish striking fresh water. Well, I pointed out last year, and I point out again to-day, that the whole area allotted to seiners last year consists of brackish waters, and any of those who understand anything about these waters, those who are in the habit of passing between Victoria and Vancouver, must have seen in daylight at least the line of demarcation between the fresh waters and the brackish waters from the Fraser river. That line is many miles out from the mouth of the Fraser river, so that when he says that the fish struck fresh water and were picked up by the seines, I maintain that such is not the case, because the seines operated entirely in brackish water. The fresh waters of the Fraser river go for miles into the gulf before being completely absorbed by the salt water.
I wish to show that the fishermen have been deprived this year of their livelihood. I pointed out in my letter to the minister that 80 gill netters had picked up in one day's operation some 1,985 fish, or an average of about 26 fish for each individual boat, and I also pointed out that seven seines had taken between 7,000 and 8,000 fish on the same day, averaging 1,000 fish to the boat. That is only one day's operation, but there were

Salmon Fishery-Mr, Reid
days when the seine boats scooped up 8,000 and 9,000 fish; and I have it on the best authority that there was one day when the seine boats scooped up so many fish that the canneries could not use the fish and many were dumped overboard. That information I believe was given at a meeting of representatives held in New Westminster, and Mr. Found, the acting deputy, was present when that statement was made. However, the interesting and I think serious point is that in 1932 before the seine boats were allowed to operate the daily catch of the fishermen ran all the way from 100 to 500 fish per day. It is true that these fish caught in that period were low priced fish, but the fishermen have to take all that they can get as every little helps. But when the seines came in last fall and were allowed to operate in the mouth of the Fraser river the catch dropped to as low a figure as I have mentioned, about 10 fish per day. Not only so, but there were some varieties of fish that did not go up the reaches of the Fraser river-different varieties from the pink. There is a variety known as the white spring salmon which fetches a price of from 1 to 2 cents per pound, and in 1933 after the seines'started to operate not one white spring salmon went up the Fraser river. The seines scooped up not only the pink salmon but every other variety, and this helped in large measure to deplete the earnings that would otherwise have been gained by the individual gill net fishermen.
Let me now discuss prices for a moment; I will come to the question of quality afterwards. I am taking the different points in sequence so that a proper picture may be presented to the government. The minister is not correct when he states in his letter that the seine boats got a higher price for their fish than did the gill netters. If he had said that the seine boats got a higher price for their fish than the gill netters who were operating right up the Fraser river, I think he would have been accurate. But it is not true to say that the price was the same to all gill netters, because those gill netters who went out on the gulf to fish received exactly the same price as the seiners received. The price started at about 9 cents and dropped, as the season went on, to 4 cents, but all gill net fishboats that went out in that area to fish received exactly the same price from the canners as was given to the seiners. It is therefore not correct to state that the seine boats received a better price for their fish, the inference being, I suppose, that they received that better price because the fish
they caught were of better quality. On September 21 the price of salmon had dropped to 4 cents, and that was given to both the gill netters and the seine boats. The price dropped to two cents for the fish caught up the river.
But there is another variety of fish called cohoe salmon for which a price of four cents a pound was being paid, and that was paid ' to all boats irrespective of whether they were gill netters or seine boats and irrespective, of whether the fish were caught in the mouth of the Fraser river or up in the Fraser river itself.
At one period of the fishing season last year there was a glut of fish and when the canneries were offering our fishermen one and a half to two cents, not per pound but apiece, but for whole salmon weighing ten to fourteen pounds, the fishing interests just across the line in the United States were paying fifteen cents apiece for pinks, and some of our fishermen took their catches across the line and received from the canning interests in the state of Washington, in some instances, four times the price they were being offered in British Columbia and in particular prices in the Fraser river area.
Coming, now, to quality, I maintain that there is no difference in the fish caught in the mouth of the river whether by gill netters or by seiners. The mouth of the Fraser river is brackish water. If the fish were caught away out in the open, such as around the gulf islands, there might be some difference. In the gulf islands and the surrounding area the salmon would be caught in pure salt water, but in the area allotted to the seiners last year, the waters were very entirely brackish and the price paid as I have stated for fish caught by gill netters in that area was the same as that paid to the seine fishermen.
I should like now to quote prices paid in the United States and those paid in British Columbia, and I took note that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) was quoting various commodities produced in this country by Canadians, for which we received more for, he omitted to mention the product of one of our greatest industries, that is fish, because the price given to the fishermen in the state of Washington just across the border from us was far greater than that given to the fishermen on the Fraser river. For instance, the price of spring salmon was six cents a pound; this year the price of sockeye salmon was fifty cents apiece, the first year I suppose that sockeye salmon have been just a little lower in the United States. In other years United
Salmon Fishery-Mr. Reid

at least to those of us who know the situation out there, that this meant, " Well, we hope that these fish that were turned down were caught by gill netters, so that we can circumvent the arguments that probably will be used by the hon. member for New Westminster against the order in council which we passed allowing seine boats to operate in the mouth of the river."
To get down to it, Mr. Speaker, I am asking that the order in council be rescinded. I am asking that seine boats be not allowed in the mouth of the Fraser river, that they be entirely removed. Seine boats I might say move from one area to another; they are just like birds of prey, if one could use that expression in connection with fish, because immediately they fish out one area they move to another, and when that is scooped out they are off to still another. If this is allowed to go on they will not only destroy all the fish in the Fraser river but also will throw over 2,000 men out of employment.
Now let us consider the question of quality. If it is a question of quality why not allow the men on the Fraser river to put up a pack and call it the Fraser river pack? Above the Fraser river bridge we have some 228 fishermen operating, many of whom put up small smokehouses this year, gutted and smoked these pink salmon and peddled them around the country, thereby picking up quite a few dollars. If the seiners are allowed to operate these 228 fishermen will have no pink salmon in future and, as I said before, if they are allowed to go on there will be no sockeye salmon either, because the late run of the sockeye salmon is going to be picked up this year by the 50 or 60 seine boats operating in British Columbia waters.
If it is a question of catching the fish a little more cheaply I would ask the minister why not allow the gill net fishermen to have a longer net. That could be allowed out in the mouth of the Fraser river, if not in the river itself. In Puget sound the gill net fishermen are allowed nets up to 1,800 feet in length, but in this country they are limited to 900 feet. Why not allow the fishermen nets as long as they care to use? Let them go out in the gulf with the longer nets, if it is a case of trying to lower the cost of getting the fish.
There is another point. The fishermen should be allowed to sell their fish in the highest market. I think earnest attention should be paid to the fact that last fall some of our cannerymen went to the United States and brought in one hundred thousand sockeye salmon. When prices are a little lower

apparently it is all right for the cannery men to go across the line and bring in the somewhat cheaper fish in order to hammer down the Canadian fishermen, but when prices are higher-and in fact every year- our fishermen are precluded by our laws and regulations from exporting fresh sockeye salmon. The whole concern seems to be for the cannerymen and not for the fishermen. We are paying out money for relief; we are endeavouring to encourage employment, but at the same time this government is passing regulations which put hundreds of men out of employment. If it is a case of the greatest good for the greatest number look at the figures I have quoted. Even allowing eight men to a boat the seine boats will employ at most 500 men, as against 2,058 individual fishermen who are endeavouring to earn their livelihood on the Fraser river. If Canada cannot compete with the United States interests-and I say this frankly-it is because the cannery interests in British Columbia have too much overhead; the industry is overloaded or over capitalized, if I may use that word. The result, as I have endeavoured to show, is the lowest possible price they can give the fishermen.
I am appealing to the government and to the minister to repeal this order in council. I appeal to him also, especially when the house is in session, to have the committee deal with any further regulations that may be proposed. All matters affecting agriculture are referred to the agriculture committee, but when it comes to our fisheries, one of our most important industries, these regulations are approved and passed by order in council. Yet we have the committee on fisheries which would be only too glad to be given an opportunity to discuss these matters. I appeal to the house on behalf of more than
2,000	men whose living has been interfered with by the action of this government, and I trust that my appeal will not be in vain. If some remedy is not applied I am sure the reults will be very disastrous indeed. Not only will they deplete our fisheries but all these men will be thrown out of employment and will have their means of livelihood taken away from them. Having made these representations I ask that the government give serious consideration to the matter.

speechtext:
I think the best answer I can give my hon. friend at the moment is the report which was made by my deputy upon his return. I have also a letter from the board of inspection for British Columbia canned salmon, which gives an entirely different view from that expressed to-day by my hon. friend as to the quality of the fish caught after they leave the sea and enter the Fraser river. These reports state very clearly that the fish caught in the river has lost its quality and become of second or third grade, and if the regulation had not been adopted there would have been a real loss to the country, because the purse seining in the gulf of Georgia has shown the best results for the industry in general. I think the report of my deputy minister should be placed before the house:
Purse-Seining for Pink and Late Run Sockeye Salmon in the Gulf of Georgia
Two species of salmon-pinks and late run sockeye-deteriorate in quality speedily as soon as they come into contact with fresh-water. Every second year there is a large run of pinks and every fourth year of late run sockeyes to the Fraser river. These fish come in mainly through the United States waters of Juan de Fuea strait and the gulf of Georgia. They are in prime condition when there and there is a large fishery for them on the United States side.
The Fraser river waters follow a well-defined course almost across the gulf of Georgia and the fish begin to go off quality as soon as they enter these waters and become speedily worse as they ascend the river. The Fraser river gill-net fishermen operate not only in the river, but out into the gulf in the Fraser river waters there.
There is a comparatively small area south of these waters and north of the boundary line in which there has been practically no gillnetting, and in which these salmon are still in prime condition.
Particularly since the canned salmon inspection regulations became effective two years ago there has been little demand for these fish for canning purposes after they enter the Fraser. Hence the position was that if they were not allowed to be taken in seines in the small area north of the boundary line and south of the Fraser river waters, they would not be caught on the Canadian side to any large extent and so we would be giving additional protection to a run of fish that was being utilized mainly by the United States. Hence, last year it was decided to allow purse-seining in this small area. This did not prevent gill-netting where it was previously conducted, and only interfered with it to the extent that the fisli would be caught before entering that area. The regulation has worked pretty much as we expected as is evidenced by the attached copy of a report of November 2, 1933, by the Canned Salmon Inspection Board, on the subject.
Last fall, when the undersigned was in British Columbia, he met a large delegation representing the Fraser river fishermen. He read to them the attached report and stated the case as frankly and clearly as he could. He explained that there was really no departure from the department's policy of encouraging gill-nets where that method of fishing was practicable, but we were faced here with the fact that if fishing were restricted to gill-nets we would get little advantage from it. Hence the Fraser river gill-netters could not be hurt so much by the regulation owing to the small demand for this fish when taken in the river, and they might fish for them, if they rvished, as they did in the past.
The undersigned did use the figures that were given to him at the time as to the total pack of seine caught fish from this area that was put up, which he stated w-as approximately
100,000	cases. It has since been developed that these figures included the whole pack put up in district No. 1, no matter where the fish were caught. The figures were, therefore, too large. This does not change the validity of the argument itself as to the propriety in the public interest of this regulation. The fact that last season there vrere 524,369 cases of pink salmon packed in British Columbia, that of these 13,930 were classed by the inspection board as "Second Quality" and that 11,142 of these "Second Quality" fish were from Fraser river gill-net caught pinks, while only 185 cases of fish taken in purse-seines in the southern area were so classed, speaks for itself.

I should like also to put on record the report made by the board of inspection for British Columbia canned salmon. It is dated November 2, 1933, and is contained in a letter addressed to Mr. Motherwell, chief supervisor of fisheries, at Vancouver:
Dear Sir,
Replying to your letter of the 28th ultimo regarding pinks in the Fraser river district.
The opening of waters off the Fraser to seining would appear to have led to a much improved quality in respect to a large portion of the pack at Fraser river canneries and tanneries in the Vancouver area packing so-called Fraser river pinks. The individual experience of each member of the board over a long period of years has been that the great bulk of the Fraser pink pack has been of such a character that under the inspection now in force it would have to be classed as second quality for lack of firmness. It was only the very early portion of the pack that would have been approved. This season it has been evident that a large part of the catch came from outside waters having firmness and colour never evident in pinks gill-netted in the fresh [DOT] water of the river.
The board had no information regarding each parcel as to whether packed from seined or gill-netted pinks and so can deal with the question in only a general way but is of opinion that the regulations for inspection acted as a deterrent on the packing of gill-netted pinks, and that in the case of those that were packed there was more care in most cases to cull out males and other defective fish, so that while the parcels which failed' of approval were soft, there was not much of the "soupy" fish that will pour out of a can which has been much in evidence in previous pink packs on the Fraser.
The published figures of the pack of pinks in the Fraser river area at time of writing are 142,948 cases. While these have not yet all been submitted for inspection and include some fish brought in from Johnston straits which may or may not have been heading for the Fraser, there have been of those examined only 11,000 cases relegated to second quality.
The pack of Fraser pinks in 1929 which was the last year when they were packed in quantity consisted of 161,529 cases. The result of the packing of that fish was a demoralization of the market and a loss of prestige for British Columbia pink salmon, one of the results being that in 1931, which was the next cycle year when pinks come into the Fraser, there were packed only 20.000. If the pack of 1929, consisting of 161,529 cases had been submitted to the inspection system now in vogue the board considers it safe to say there would have been at least 100,000 cases degraded to second quality.
The board considers that seining the fish in the gulf before they suffer from contact with the brackish water, has resulted in the production of at least 100,000 cases of creditable fish which if not caught in the gulf but allowed to enter the river would, if taken, have been unfit to pack or have resulted in the same quantity of a low grade product.
The bulk of the pinks packed in British Columbia this season has already been sold,

there being a good market demand, and what is being delivered instead of besmirching the reputation of Canadian salmon as did the Fraser pack of 1929, will raise it and the consuming centres will be in a receptive mood for subsequent packs.
Yours truly,
Board of Inspection for British Columbia Canned Salmon,
E. O. Cornish,
Chairman.
I do not think I need add very much to the statement of my deputy minister and the one made by this board. All I can say is that this government desires, just as much as my hon. friend does, to help the fishermen of the Fraser river, providing no harm is done to the industry in general. I think the regulation which was passed has proved itself to be beneficial to the industry on the Pacific coast without injuring the interests of the fishermen on the Fraser river. As is proved by these reports, the fish taken is of second quality. The catches in the river fell down considerably from 1929 to 1931. My hon. friend is representing the fishermen and I understand the position he takes in this house. But he sees only one side of the question while the government has to look to the best interests of the industry as a whole. We consider that what has been done is in the best interests of the industry.

I am aware of the

speechtext: I am stating it now.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine

I assure my hon.
friend that this regulation was put in force only after the question had been thoroughly studied. In view of the report and letters we have received from the Pacific coast, it is not at the moment the intention of the government to modify or repeal this regulation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to take part in this debate but the Acting Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Duranleau) has referred to the report of the inspection board. My suggestion is that he should tear up that report or put it in the fire. When writing to the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) the hon. minister made the statement that the results of the investigation were not far different

Salmon Fishery-Mr. Neill
from what was anticipated. Of course they were not far different, they were made to fit the circumstances. What does the report of this board of inspection amount to? It is simply if and when and perhaps and maybe; it is simply an attempt to justify the policy laid down by the department. They admit that they cannot distinguish between fish caught in the one place and those caught in another; the whole thing is an ex parte statement of the most ridiculous character. They refer to the last big catch in 1929 and suggest that it was the quality of the catch that demoralized the whole market. Was it the quality of that local catch that demoralized the world trade in salmon? We all know that such a thing is ridiculous and such a statement is unworthy of being included in a report of that kind. In 1929 there was a demand for fish of any kind, as long as it had a fin on it it was good enough to go into a can. But then the world debacle took place and you could not sell salmon of any quality at any price. The following year there was a very small catch, practically no chums. But had that anything to do with the quality? I did not catch the whole of the report, but as I understood it it was simply made on request and intended merely to support an announced and agreed on policy. The figures collected by the board and furnished to Major Motherwell and passed on by him to Doctor Found were not the same as Doctor Found presented to the meeting at New Westminster. Yet he should have had the report before him.
I think the minister would have been well advised not to have said that the policy of the department is to curtail seining wherever possible. I know that has been the announced policy of the department but the department has given little indication of carrying it out of late years. It is very unfortunate that this particular local policy should be adopted in these days of unemployment. Wrap it up, go around it, evade the issue as you like, there is no question that it has resulted in a very serious curtailment of employment of fishermen. That result will continue in the future.
We do not seem to be able to agree as to whether there was 100,000 or 500,000 cases put up, but the board of inspection says that they were of real good quality. If that is the case, why is it that there have been so many pinks condemned in the last few months? Let the minister go and check up the reports which have been made recently. If he does that. I think he will receive quite a surprise.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING

speechtext:
This board of inspection made an ex parte statement in the month of October, but how many salmon had been inspected at that time? They seemed to have the whole thing cut and dried and knew just what the quality was going to be. I think I am safe in suggesting that they had not inspected a third of the catch at that time.
The statement made quite frequently by the hon. member for New Westminster would seem to be the crux of the whole matter. He stated that seiners were allowed to fish right in the mouth of the Fraser river. The minister has said that a small area had been set aside right down on the boundary line where the gill-netters do not penetrate and where the water was not muddy. He stated that the seiners could operate there quite successfully.
I believe there is a certain amount of truth in that, but this area is small and right down on the American fishing borderline. Had the seining been confined to that area there might have been some justification for the argument advanced by the department that a better quality of fish could be caught by being taken earlier in seines, but they made a mistake when they threw open the whole mouth of the river to the seiners. This is the area of muddy water and the gill-netters operate there and as far out as the muddy water extends. I do not suppose they went down as far as this small area, but the mistake was in not confining the seiners to that small area. The minister refers to this existing district as a small area but it is not small and the seiners were given access to a territory contiguous or belonging to the gill-netters, so to speak. The minister has suggested in his letter to the hon. member that there is a possibility of changing the area boundary this year, but why should not this have been done in the beginning? It is just like the 24-hour rule which was found to be impracticable. If our advice had been listened to last year this matter would have been brought before the fishing committee where representations could have been made. The mistake made in this instance was in giving the seiners certain territory which came within the jurisdiction of the gill-netters. The minister has said that the gill-netters could go down there and operate but if he were one he would know What kind of a chance he would have operating among seiners.
I wish to endorse the representations made by the hon. member for New Westminster as regards the deputy minister not having meetings out there. That policy was inaugurated nearly ten years ago; I never heard anyone complain about it, except those who wanted to protect special interests. It was a fair thing and there were no objections. The
Salmon Fishery-Mr. Neill

present Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) went out there, and there was a sort of understanding that he should hear the representations of one class only; it was understood that he would be dined by the canners and would hear their side of the matter. But very much to his credit he insisted on staying over a couple of days in order to hear the point of view of the fishermen themselves. He did so and listened to them as attentively as he had listened to the other side, and he got a very much better perspective of the situation by hearing both sides than he would have got if he had listened to the representations of the canners alone, listening to what they had to say and then going home and acting upon it. And when the deputy came out from year to year he also gave a fair hearing to all sides. A better arrangement could not be conceived. Of course, big interests can always send delegations here, just as they did last January when the twenty-four hour rule was put into effect overnight. But the fishermen cannot do this. We can voice their grievance after it has become a grievance, or we can voice their views privately to the deputy. But that is a very different thing from the deputy going out and getting the consensus of opinion from all concerned. I do not know why the deputy was instructed not to have meetings this year. I venture to suggest that he was ashamed to have any meetings. I suggest that these meetings should be continued in the future.
There is another thing I might suggest. It is beside the point, but I have been thinking somewhat of it of late. Perhaps with the good offices of the minister, whose name would go down in history so far as the fishing industry in British Columbia is concerned, would it not be a good thing, would not this be the appropriate time, to inaugurate in connection with that industry a policy such as has been adopted in the United States and which is indicated by the letters N.I.R.A. Instead of the canners believing that the only way they can achieve success is to put something over the fishermen, by cutting down their prices unfairly, by compelling them to deal with local interests, and so on, and instead of the fishermen having a determined prejudice against anything that the cannery men might suggest, merely because it comes from them, would this not be a favourable moment, with the assistance of the minister, if he were impartial in the matter, to try to get together rather than to have the different parties concerned pulling in opposite directions? Why not have a proper basis of prices? The United States has a wage code. Suppose we could arrange a code with regard 
to the price of fish and then cooperate along these lines. Above all, let the cannery men do what they are best fitted for, what is essentially their business, namely, the canning of fish, and let the fishermen attend to their business, let them do what they are best fitted for, which is the catching of the fish. That arrangement was carried out a number of years ago in connection with halibut. I have only a vague understanding of it, but I believe that at one time the buying interests, those who buy halibut and ship it to the New York market, were in the business of fishing, and their boats were competing with what I would call the independent fishermen. This led to all kinds of trouble, jealousy and ill will, until finally the practice was abandoned and the buyers confined themselves to their legitimate business of buying and selling halibut, leaving the fishermen to do the fishing. That system has worked well, neither side having tried to hold up the other. If we could adopt something like N.I.RA. in connection with the fishing industry on the Pacific coast it would be a monument to the minister and to everyone connected with it, and it would be very much to the benefit of all classes. No one class would benefit unduly and there would be a fair deal all round. The fishermen would realize the troubles of the cannery men and the cannery men would understand that it was in the best interests of the industry to deal fairly with the fishermen, so that it would not be a question of cutting each other's throats. The minister might seriously consider this proposal, and anything I can do to assist him I should be glad to do. I shall be happy to devote my time and energies to helping him to carry out something of this sort on the coast, if he will give it his endorsement and see to it that some active measures are adopted to have it inaugurated.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
I would not intervene but
for the fact that, in the first place, I come from British Columbia and have a fairly good knowledge of the situation and secondly because as Minister of Trade and Commerce I am interested in this matter, which in a measure affects the work of the department over which I preside.
The two hon. members opposite who have spoken on the subject have quite earnestly, and certainly very vigorously, advanced what they believe to be the interests of the fishermen. I submit however that there has been rather a disregard of certain facts which are beyond the control of government or of man, for that matter. Let me say at once that as

Salmon Fishery-Mr. Stevens
far as I am concerned-and I know the view of the Acting Minister of Fisheries and of the government generally-we are just as much interested in the welfare and prosperity of the fishermen on the Fraser river or in any other section of Canada as are the hon. gentlemen opposite. But the government, in the administration of this matter, like their predecessors in office, both the preceding government and other governments for the last thirty years, have always been confronted with certain stubborn facts, which I will refer to in the course of my remarks.
The hon. member for New Westminster made certain comparisons indicating a diminution of catch by fishermen on the Fraser river. That the house may be better seized of the tremendous changes that have taken place on the Fraser river, let me give some of my own recollections. I can recall when, long before the hon. member for New Westminster came to that district, one could go out to Steveston on a Sunday evening after the weekend holiday-the fishermen laid up for twenty-four hours in those days-and see from 6,000 to 7,000 fishing boats leaving Steveston alone, going to the sand flats at the mouth of the river to fish. Furthermore, in those days, especially in every fourth year when the large run occurred, most of these fishermen would make a very profitable catch. I think I am correct in saying that for many years in the early stages of the industry the canneries in the Fraser river area put up by long odds the largest portion of the catch.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: In British Columbia.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
Yes. Gradually that pack diminished and the northern areas, which are of a different character, became the predominant locality in which salmon was packed. Now, what brought about the change? I think we ought to get this clearly before the house, and if hon, members will bear with me I will make one or two references to some of the facts relating to this matter.
In the first place, it must be remembered that the Fraser river is one of the large rivers flowing into the Pacific, on the upper reaches of which salmon are spawned. I suppose the Fraser river, the Columbia river, the Stikine, and some of the northern rivers as well as some of the smaller streams, the Skagit river and others, are the sources which maintain the supply of salmon. Salmon on the Fraser river are peculiar in this respect that the sockeyes usually have what is known as the heavy run once every four years. One of the phenomena of the world is the way in 7472ft-48|
which the sockeye salmon have an extraordinary run every four years; that is a much larger number come up the river to spawn. Then of course the spawn goes out to sea and it is a peculiar characteristic of our salmon that they go out, nobody knows where, remain there for a certain time and then return to the stream where they were spawned Nature in a most extraordinary manner provides the instinct which brings this about. It has been one of the duties and cares of all governments to maintain the spawning grounds in as good shape as possible, very frequently, by the installation of hatcheries, taking eggs where available from the fish when in proper condition and depositing them in hatcheries, supplementing the efforts of nature in maintaining the run of salmon in the Fraser river.
During the construction of the Canadian National a huge blast was set off in the Fraser canyon throwing into the river, I suppose, millions of tons of rock from the side of the mountain. This for several years caused an interference with the run of the fish up the river. It was soon discovered and not this particular government, but preceding governments spent very large sums of money, I have forgotten the amount, in clearing away this barrier in the Fraser so that the fish might run up. It did, however, have the most damaging effect upon the fishing industry in the Fraser river, as became apparent in the recurring four-year periods by the fact that there was a rapid diminution owing, experts said, to a sufficient number of fish not being able to get up the river to spawn during a certain period. That difficulty was overcome and then efforts were made to obtain spawn and thus maintain the fisheries, but there was a serious falling off in the supply of salmon on the Fraser. So much for nature.
But another factor entered into the situation. It must be borne in mind that when the salmon go out to sea to their habitat wherever that may be, and return to the place where they were spawned, in this case the Fraser river, they come round the gulf of Georgia, round the southern end of Vancouver island-a number go north-through the strait of Juan de Fuca; then they strike the mainland coast and come up the coast from the state of Washington into the area of British Columbia and up the Fraser. The Fraser is a huge river, over a thousand miles in length; it constantly pours into the gulf of Georgia a muddy water that carries in suspension a fine silt. When the river empties into the gulf of Georgia, the working of tides up and down the gulf carries the fresh water to a certain extent up the coast, but chiefly

Salmon Fishery-Mr. Stevens
down, so I would suppose-and I am speaking just from memory-for probably forty miles down the coast will be found silt deposits of the Fraser. This in centuries and millenniums has built up wide flats, what we call tidal flats or shallow areas. I am informed that the fish go out into very deep sea and when they come in they are hard, firm and of very fine quality, but again obeying the dictates of nature, they hover around river mouths in that brackish water of which the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) has spoken. There they remain for a certain period until their physical condition is suitable, shall I sa3', to the necessities of spawning. After hovering there for a certain period, they go up the river to the spawning beds, very many of them going long distances up the main river and its tributaries. I can recall in the early days when the Fraser river would be almost choked with the numbers of salmon ascending, and they may still be seen in large numbers going up the river and its tributaries. But during the period, which may be a few days or longer, they are lying in the brackish ^waters, they gradually softem; their flesh becomes soft and they deteriorate from the standpoint of edibility. Therefore the sooner the fish can be caught after they arrive from the deep sea water in the shallow areas along the coast, the better their condition will be.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: The statement was made at a meeting that the fish caught long ago, that is when there were six or seven thousand millions at the mouth of the Fraser, were just as good as they are to-day.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
I am coming to an explanation of that point. In part my hon. friend is correct, but not wholly so. The point I am making for the moment is that the sooner the fish are caught after they come into shallow water, the better, and the longer they remain there, the softer they become. No one will dispute that fact.
Another factor enters into the matter. During the years our United States friends-and in saying what I am about to say, I am not criticizing them; that is their business-knowing these fish come right by their door to enter the Fraser and not having very much interest in that river, simply set themselves to catch as many salmon as they could while they were in waters adjacent to their own territory. I think I am correct in saying that 90 per cent of the fish that run up the Canadian waters of the Fraser would for many miles pass United States territory contiguous to British Columbia. What is the result? Huge canneries developed at Belling-

ham, Blaine and other places just south of the boundary and the United States authorize not only gill net fishing, which is done in a comparatively small way, but the installation of fish traps and) seines. A fish trap is one of the most murderous contrivances ever invented so far as catching fish is concerned. It consists of long reaches of piling with nets stretched along. My hon. friends will correct me if I am stating this inaccurately. I think in some cases a mile or perhaps more of this will be stretched out crossing the known pathway of the fish. As the fish sweep up the coast and strike one of these barriers which are placed at an angle across the pathway they are following, they are guided into what is known as a trap, a trap being quite a huge area of piling with nets down quite deep so that there is no possibility of the fish escaping once they are in it. When they are in the trap, they are lifted out of it by machinery and literally hundreds of tons of fish are taken out of traps in that way. I have seen this and have no doubt hon. members have seen pictures of it. It is a most murderous system of fishing, but it is followed quite commonly and has been to my knowledge for the last ten years.
That is as far as trap fishing is concerned. Then they have another system of fishing with purse seines, a huge net, the dimensions of which are obtainable from the department,- I do not carry them in my mind. This net is thrown out in deep water. When they sight a shoal or when they know that fish are running,-and the men become very skilful at that,-they throw out one of these nets. It is very long, a boat will run in a circle and when a large section of this net is out it is gradually drawn together and pulled tight at the bottom and the whole net drawn into the boat; and fish are taken out by the ton, not individual fish as in gill net and similar forms of fishing. This purse seine fishing is carried on very extensively by our American friends. That again is not a point I am criticizing, it is just a statement of fact. It is done by them before the fish reach Canadian waters at all, before they get near the Fraser river.
A few years ago the government of Canada, largely at the instigation of the government of British Columbia and the fishing interests generally there, worked out what is known as the Sockeye Salmon treaty. This treaty has been discussed pro and con. In any case it was signed and passed this parliament, but it has never been ratified by the United States congress, and therefore is not in effect. The object of the treaty was to deal with this situation, which in British Columbia was felt

Salmon Fishery-Mr. Stevens
to be unfair, because we were spending thousands of dollars to maintain the quantity of fish spawned in the Fraser by supplementing nature with hatcheries, we were restricting our own fishermen so that a certain number of fish could escape up the river for spawning, but while we were doing that our American friends by a system of trap and 'purse seine fishing were taking unlimited quantities of fish. Had the Sockeye Salmon treaty become effective it would to a substantial degree have rectified this condition, but it has not been ratified and we are faced with the stubborn facts. The catch on the Fraser river fell off year by year until in 1931 it was, I think, only 20,000 cases. My hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Reid) knows these figures probably more accurately than I. At any rate the catch had fallen to a lamentable degree.
Then the suggestion was made that, inasmuch as there was apparently no possibility of a modus vivendi with the United States, this treaty which we had passed in good faith not having been ratified by the American senate, why should not Canadian interests be permitted to seine in the parallel area on the Canadian side? I admit very frankly that it is a matter for debate whether purse seining should or should not be allowed. I ask my hon. friends to accept that as a fair statement, but not an admission that the whole thing is wrong, I do not want to be so interpreted. However I can see their side of the question. I submit that if the facts as I have stated them are accurate-and I think no one will question them-then it stands to reason that the Canadians might just as well catch a certain amount of fish with seines in the same manner as the Americans do and thus increase the quantity of fish that we can put up. That is on the one hand. On the other hand I think it is demonstrated beyond any question that the fish so caught are of a superior quality to those caught in the river. I will admit with my hon. friend from New Westminster that such gill net boats or individual fishermen as go out of the mouth of the river and fish on the sand heads may catch fish practically equal in quality to those caught by the seiners, but I think generally speaking those caught by the seiners are superior. As my hon. friend knows, you will see fishermen fishing with their gill nets above the Fraser river bridge, twenty miles from the mouth of the river, but in that area from the mouth of the river to as high as the gill net fishermen operate, there will be a larger proportion of soft or inferior fish than would be caught outside the mouth of the river. Therefore I think it cannot be questioned that the fish caught by the seine fishermen in the area referred to in
this order in council are of a firmer and superior quality.
Another thing I want to say-and which to my mind is of greater importance than almost any other point-is that we have in British Columbia salmon fisheries a very fine industry. Perhaps I should say we had, because it was better years ago than it is to-day. But we still have in the salmon fisheries an important industry. However, the competition that we are now confronted with is much keener than it was ten or twenty or thirty years ago. Some years ago our only competition came from the Americans, and at first they competed with us only on Puget Sound. I remember very well when there were very few American canneries in the north. But gradually the American interests extended their canneries in Alaska, where they catch a very fine type of sockeye as well as other kinds of salmon, sockeye being the most attractive for the market. One of my hon. friends said a moment ago that he could not see why Canadian packers could not compete successfully with the American, but my hon. friend must at least do the Canadian packers this justice, that the salmon packed in Alaska, as well as in northern British Columbia, are generally speaking in better condition when caught, owing to the water being colder and clearer, than those caught at the mouth of the Fraser or of the Columbia. Inasmuch as the American pack is largely an Alaska pack we are therefore faced with keener competition from Americans to-day than we were twenty or twenty-five years ago. That is one point. Then in the last ten years the Japanese have come on the world market, they now catch salmon on the Siberian coast and the Asiatic coast quite similar, and quite as good, I am told by those competent to judge, as the Alaska and northern British Columbia salmon. In fact they are the same general type of fish.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: By what method do they kill them?

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
I think methods very
similar to ours.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
By traps or purse
seines?

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
They use the traps the
same as we do, I do not know whether they are precisely the same, but I think in effect they are the same. I omitted to say that traps are used very freely in Alaska, and they are used in British Columbia waters in one or two cases. The Japanese came on the market, and they have been our keenest competitors in the European markets. Then

Salmon Fishery-Mr. Stevens
within the last five years the Russians have come into the picture, with very extensive government owned and established canneries, and to-day they are amongst our keenest factors in the world market for salmon.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: If I might interrupt, my contention was that price is the predominant factor in Great Britain.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
Quite so. I am glad my
hon. friend mentioned that. I was saying that the Japanese and Russians being now in the picture are tremendously keen competitors not only in respect of quality but of quantity. The price competition is accentuated by the presence of these two additional competitors, particularly the Russians. They have made it extremely difficult to sell our fish in the world markets. These facts are inescapable, they are factors beyond our control, and they cannot be lightly brushed aside. We must face them; we must recognize them. What the government of the day are trying to do is this: We are tlying to maintain the high standard of Canadian salmon, and we dare not allow the conditions that obtained in 1930 or 1931 to return. In those years quite a substantial quantity of very inferior fish were packed and placed on the market, and I know that as Minister of Trade and Commerce I received some very very strong protests. Speaking from memory I recall one large distributor who said that he would never take any more British Columbia salmon. In any case we know that it did injure our reputation, and it is with the desire to win back and maintain the excellent reputation we have had on the world market in years gone by that these regulations were brought into force.
Let me say first-and I say this to my hon. friend from New Westminster very courteously-that I do not think any further diminution of the catch by gill net fishermen has resulted from the use of purse seines in the area to which the order in council refers than would have obtained if we had done nothing and simply allowed matters to take their course. I would go further. If there has been a slight diminution-and I do not think there has been very much-we are making up for it in the better condition of the fish and in being able to meet the keener competition I have just mentioned.
Then I was going to say a further word with reference to the other order in council which was passed and later repealed. My hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) spoke in rather scathing terms of that order in council. I recall that he protested at the time, but I want to say that it was an effort

to meet a condition which I think is inimical to the best interests of the canned salmon industry. I will give an illustration of that. A certain individual had a cannery in the harbour of Vancouvex-, which obviously is not the place for a cannery except to take fish locally. Not being able to get fish locally, he encouraged men to go away into the north-and we had abundant evidence that they went for several hundred miles- and there buy up fish and bring them down to Vancouver to this cannery, so that when the fish reached the cannery they were several days old. I am sure that neither of my hon. friends will assert for a moment that fish handled under those conditions are calculated to give the best results in our canning operations; indeed, sir, it is a menace to the canning industry. I do not want to say that the man who builds a cannery in the harbour of Vancouver should not be given a chance to live, but there is reason in all these things. A man who will build his cannery there and expect to get his fish from around Rivers inlet or the Skeena river, is foolish. He should not be encouraged, and it is obvious that he has no claim on any government for protection or assistance. If he were getting his fish at his pier certainly he should be entitled to every consideration, but the effort should be to get the fish to the cannery as quickly as possible after they arc caught.
Let me remind my hon. friend of another matter, and I do not refer to this because I am a Conservative and the government to which I am going to refer was Liberal, but rather in order to give the point of view that was taken by a government in which undoubtedly he would have confidence, and in order to disabuse his mind of any thought that the action was taken by a government whose whole outlook was out of sympathy with his own. During the entire period Sir Wilfrid Laurier was in power there was a very strict boat rating system in operation in British Columbia, and what was the boat rating system? It was a most ai'bitrary system. In the light of all that has passed I am not prepared to say that it was not the best system, although I fought it when I first came to parliament nearly twenty-three years ago. Under that system the Department of Marine and Fisheries, as it was then, without any particular rule but in an arbitrary fashion allocated to each cannery a certain number of boats. I think it ran from about twenty-five boats to fifty or sixty, and the average would be about forty. The cannery secured the allocation of boats, and then it allowed certain individual fishermen to take

Salmon Fishery-Mr. Stevens
the cannery boats and fish, but no one could fish in the area contiguous to that cannery and allocated to it but the boats of the cannery itself. In other words, under the regulations that obtained for about a score of years, the cannery had an absolute monopoly of the fishing in the area in which the cannery was located. I am not prepared to say that this was wrong; after seeing free fishing in operation all over the coast, with the grief, the trials, the tribulations and losses that have occurred, I am inclined to think that some such system in operation to-day might have a better result. For instance, a moment ago the hon. member for Comox-Alberni asked why the acting minister did not adopt something along the line of the N.R.A. in the United States. That is precisely what the N.R.A. is doing to-day; they are simply restricting the competition in business, shall I say, insisting upon an arrangement between business and workers, and arbitrarily controlling it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: But not on one end only; on both ends.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
Of course, but the N.R.A., applied to the canning industry on the Pacific coast, would result substantially in something such as I have mentioned. I must say, however, that looking back over the years I am not now' prepared wholly to condemn that system, but certainly that system was condemned by those who held the view now held! by my hon. friend. I condemned it; I argued) for open fishing along the Pacific coast long before my hon. friend came to the house. We achieved that change, but the intricacies of the business and the factors entering into it, which I mentioned a moment ago-^the competition from the United States the use by United States fishermen of traps and purse seines, the fact that they had the first chance at the fish before they get into Canadian waters, the fact that competition from Russia and Japan must be faced in the world market, the gradual diminution due to heavy fishing on the Fraser river and so on-all have tended to make the industry less profitable than it was twenty-five, thirty or thirty-five years ago, as I saw it in the early days when I first went to British Columbia.
I think the only quarrel I would have with the two hon. members who have spoken is with regard to their attack upon the Acting Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Duranleau) because they allege that he is not interested in the fishermen and is disregarding their interests. Speaking for the government I think I can ajay that we are just as keenly interested in
the welfare of the fishermen as my hon. friends are, but we cannot ignore those factors to which I have referred, which undoubtedly play an important part in connection with the industry as a whole.
I have just one word in conclusion. My hon. friend from New Westminster rather taunted me, I thought. It was rather cleverly done and nicely placed upon Hansardi, so that he can read it to his friends on the Fraser river and say how he told the Minister of Trade and Commerce, on the floor of the house, that he was the friend of the big interests and the packers and therefore was not a friend of the fishermen. I would like to ask my hon. friend, as a good sportsman, whether he thinks that is quite fair.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: May I point out that he did not say anything about the miners of East Kootenay.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: I do not quite see what the miners of East Kootenay have to dlo with the fishermen. I appeal to my hon. friend at least to give those of us who may differ with him credit for honestly differing. I want to tell him very candidly that I have not the slightest interest in any way-I am not talking financially but sympathetically-with the canners of British Columbia other than my interest in them as ordinary business men of the community. Here in this house, in our efforts to meet this difficult problem, and while extremely anxious to assist, in this instance, the fishermen, we must not simply escape by saying to the fishermen that the fellow who does not succeed in helping to solve their problems is failing because he is a friend of the employer or the packer or the business man. As a matter of fact, everyone from British Columbia knows perfectly well that the canning industry has had an exceedingly difficult time during the last ten years. I question if there has been any profit, or very much profit, of any kind made out of the canning industry, and certainly there has been a great deal of money lost in it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: Too much watered stock.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
There is. I say to my hon. friend very frankly that I have not an atom of sympathy with watered stock, for instance, in Canadian Canneries, and I would not have a bit of hesitancy if he brought the matter forward, to help him wring it out. While the operations of many canneries may not be paying, there are some operators in British Columbia I can assure my hon. friend who are just as honest as he is or myself, or at least as we think we. are.

Salmon Fishery-Mr. Stevens

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: The lad} doth protest too much.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
No, you will acquit me of that. We cannot make rascals out of everybody unheard, and I am not going to be a party to it. If my hon. friend (Mr. Reid) really takes any comfort out of these insinuations I shall not quarrel with him a particle, but I say that a government must take cognizance of all the facts of the case, and while we are just as anxious as he is to protect the interests of the fishermen on the Fraser river, we cannot interfere with the American operations south of the line to which I have referred, and which undoubtedly get the major portion of the fish originating in the Fraser river. Nor can we combat with nature or overcome the depletion of the fisheries due to man's operations and the falling off of production, except to the extent that we impose regulations that will protect the fish.
My hon. friend asked a moment ago why we did not allow longer gill nets, and he suggested very skilfully that these should be allowed only outside. He knows very well that with the drift net system-he knows, as well as a few others who have had the experience-that you could send half a dozen or a dozen or fifty fishermen out of Steveston with a net twice as long as the present regulations allow. They go out into the gulf, and with the ordinary drift of the incoming tide it would not be long before the nets would be across the mouth of the river, and they would block the river.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: But if the tide was going out.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: I am pointing out what could happen, and my hon. friend knows that the fishermen are just cute enough to do that, and I would not blame them for trying. But my hon. friend knows, and I as a member of the government and the minister, must remember that there must be permitted a certain amount of escape up the river.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: My hon. friend from Van-couver-Burrard (Mr. Hanbury) recognizes that. How do we give that escape? By saying that the mesh shall be of a certain size so that the smaller fish can get through. We also give them a way of escape by limiting the size of the gill net so that it will not block the river, and also by saying that they shall fish only six days in the week. We have always reserved Sunday.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: What about seine fishing?

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
I am talking about gill
nets. I say there must be a way of escape. The seine fishing is out in the open waters. I am not saying that there is not room for dispute regarding seine fishing but the seine fishermen are operating in open waters, and not across the mouth of a river. Take the dragnet system, for instance, which used to be used in my hon. friend's territory. He knows as I know, or as I did up to a few years ago when I was more closely acquainted with it, that we had constantly to watch against a man stretching his dragnet clean across the entrance to a river. It was a common trick if they could get away with it. The officers of the department are constantly on the watch for these little evasions of the regulations. Now the duty of this government, as it has been the duty of the government that preceded us and of governments in this country for the last thirty years, during which this question has come up constantly, is to see that there is a reasonable escape of fish, a reasonable chance for the fish to get into the spawning ground, and secondly to see that as far as possible there is a fair opportunity given to those in the industry to fish. Our further duty, of course, is to do everything we can to maintain our market abroad so that the standard of our fish may be such that it will compete with the catch of other countries. I submit to the hon. gentleman that, joining with my colleague the minister, we will do everything we can to protect the interests of the industry as a whole. It is a difficult question.
My hon. friend says that the fisheries committee has not been called together. I know of no reason why a few members of the fisheries committee should not call it together and discuss these matters. I am not a member of that committee; I used to be years ago, but I do not know of any reason why it could not be called, and certainly there will be no desire to put anything in the way of any useful and intelligent discussion of the industry for the benefit of all those affected.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
If I may ask the
minister a question before he sits down, I understood him to say that the canneries, or many of them, were not paying the cost of their operations. Does he mean the actual cost of operating the individual cannery or does he take into account that a large number of the canneries have many branches which are not actually operating at the moment but on which they have to pay dividends?

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
I mean both. My hon.
friend will not ask me to demonstrate with actual cases, but I am speaking from pretty

Supply-Secretary of State
general knowledge when I say that there have been seasons in the last ten years, and particularly in the last seven years, when many canneries did not pay the cost of their operations. Individual canneries and canneries which were part of a larger system of canneries did not in many cases pay the cost of their operations, and many firms actually lost on the season's operations, apart altogether from paying anything on capital investment. There has been a very serious and a very unhealthy condition in the business. Personally I think an industry that is healthy is more likely to pay better rewards to those who are working for it than an industry that is crowded and cramped even in meeting its operating expenses.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: The same is true of the fishermen. Is not that an argument for some scheme like the N.R.A.?

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
There is a good deal in
the suggestion of my hon. friend, and it would be interesting if he and a few others would work out a suggested scheme.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: It is up to the government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: Perhaps that is right too.
Motion agreed to, and the house went into committee of supply, Mr. Gobeil in the chair.

We receive many bequests
from time to time. We received a very valuable one from the estate of the late William Molson Macpherson, of Quebec. maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: What has he to do with the banks?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
His experience will be available for the benefit of not only the Department of Finance but all other departments of government. Through the years he has accumulated a remarkable knowledge of tariff structures and his services are being made available to the government. I regret that I did not anticipate the details of the discussion under this item and I have not full information before me. ivii . STEWART (Edmonton): May I say that we over here would not mourn his retirement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
