speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: His experience with respect to tariff matters will be made available to a 1 departments of government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: Is it not a fact that this gentleman has been acting for many years as an adviser on tariff matters and has been responsible for many of the blunders the government has made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: I do not propose to accept the statement of my hon. friend just as he has made it. In his estimation everything that this government does is a blunder. I am willing to go as far as saying that no doubt the government will make mistakes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: With certain advisers they are bound to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: I do not think there ever will be a perfect government. Mr. Breadner was previously the commissioner of customs and we have in the department Mr. McKinnon, who has been acting as adviser in matters of tariff and taxation. But Mr. Breadner's ripe experience has always been drawn upon by this government and I think by preceding governments.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: What is Mr. Breadner's age?

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: He is rejuvenated.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
I think he is between
seventy and seventy-one.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
He will be in receipt of a very fine pension, having enjoyed a fairly large salary in the past number of years, upon which of course he will be retired. I ask this question because I am rather curious. The government have been retiring men of sixty-five, and have been doing so pretty generally throughout the country. I have no complaint to offer in that regard, but I am curious to know why this gentleman has been transferred from the position he is in to that of adviser to the Department of Finance. With all due respect to Mr. Breadner, I submit that his qualifications must have related largely to matters affecting the tariff in the department from which he has been transferred. Just why Mr. Breadner, who is long past the age of retirement, should be transferred to another department is to me rather curious. I am going to say very frankly that Mr. Breadner and I never agreed very much on the question of tariffs. I am not complaining about that, though I should not be at all disappointed if he were removed from any connection with

Supply-Finance-Salaries
the tariff. I fail to see however where he will be of great value to my hon. friend in the finance department. When so many civil servants are being retired for the purpose of effecting greater economy, it seems to me only reasonable that this gentleman should receive the same treatment. I cannot see that he will be of very much service to the Department of Finance in the capacity of adviser.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: As regards those who have been retired: at the age of sixty-five, my hon. friend must bear in mind that those only have been retired whose services can be entirely dispensed with and whose positions need not be filled again. There have been hundreds of such oases, where men have been retired at the age of sixty-five and their positions abolished.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: That is not the case here.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: I am coming to that. Mr. .Breadner is not standing in the way of anyone's promotion in the civil service. He might have gone out with his superannuation, but -'Wether my hon. friend agrees with Mr. Breadner's point of view regarding the incidence of the tariff is beside the point; the fact is that Mr. Breadner has accumulated through the years a vast knowledge not only of the operation of indivdual tariff items but of their repercussion upon numerous other items. The tariff structure, whether one agrees with the policy of tariffs or not, has been in existence for yeaTs and will continue for many years longer. Certainly if one is to judge "by the world trend, whether it be higher or lower tariffs, we shall continue to have a tariff structure; and when you touch a tariff item, though it may look perfectly innocent, and attempt either a reduction or an increase, it is amazing to find the ramifications, in the effect on numerous other tariff items, which a slight change in one item may bring about. It is therefore to make available to the government the knowledge which Mr. Breadner has in that respect that his services can be of peculiar value, especially when it is borne in mind that his services cost the country a very small sum. We thought it in the public interest that it was far wiser, considering the trifling sum involved, t.o make his experience available to the government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
Then my
hon. friend must admit, if that argument is correct, that Mr. Breadner's successor has not the necessary qualifications and cannot be as -valuable as Mr. Breadner. Would it not
have been better, if that is so, to keep him where he was if he was so valuable in that regard?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: My hon. friend is unconsciously confusing two things. The Commissioner of Customs is an administrative officer. Assume for the sake of argument that Mr. Breadner was the best man on earth for the position-

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
We shall
have a difference of opinion on that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
Quite so; but assuming
that he was the best man on earth for the position, eventually he must be replaced. It is therefore far better that he should be replaced by a younger man who can have the benefit of the advice and experience of Mr. Breadner while Mr. Breadner is in a position to give such advice, even though he is not in the Department of National Revenue. So that to that extent it is wise to effect the change. That was the opinion of the government, and I think that their decision was wise in the circumstances. I think it is just such action as my hon. friend would have taken, notwithstanding that his views may differ from Mr Breadner's.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: Perhaps I do not hold all the views that Mr. Breadner holds with regard to the tariff, though I may say that in all my dealings with him he was always fair and I was always satisfied with him. What I cannot understand however is why he should have been transferred to his present position. Did the Minister of Finance ask to have him transferred? Who recommended that he should be put in the position he now occupies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: The committee will appreciate the fact that it would be unfair to his successor to have Mr. Breadner remain in the department where he was-

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
Agreed at
once.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: -and the only logical place for him was the Department of Finance. I would not say that any one individual I could name was responsible for his transfer, but the minister is prepared to assume the responsibility for it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: Do you approve of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: I think that on the whole it was a wise decision; I believe it was the proper course under the circumstances.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
As a member of the
government the minister had to accept it.
,	COMMONS
Supply-Finance-Salaries

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: As I understand the situation, Mr. Breadner in the past has been administering a certain department-the Department of Customs-and we know that during his administration he demonstrated a wonderful capacity for interfering with business in this country; there is no calculating how much damage he has done to the trade of the country in that position. Now he is transferred from the position, not of administering the act, but to the finance department where he will make the tariff.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
Is he not to be consulted
in framing the tariff, when the budget is drawn up?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: Not necessarily.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
Will the minister give an
example of some of the questions that will be submitted to him for advice?

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: What is his work?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
I can give an example
that has no reference at all 'to the finance department. In drawing up a treaty-

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: A treaty; precisely. He will be making the tariff.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
-the Department of External Affairs can call in Mr. Breadner and ask him, " What effect will the lowering or the raising of duties, or a change in the duties on a certain commodity or list of commodities have on trade in Canada?" And he can be asked to prepare a memorandum for the guidance of the government.
Mr. 10UNG:	He will always give you
the same answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
My hon. friend must not
get into a discussion of the relative merits of protection and free trade and that sort of thing. That is not the point. It matters not what Mr. Breadner's views or those of the government of the day may be; the information which is asked from Mr. Breadner is what the result will be if a certain action is taken. His advice whether the tariff should be raised or lowered is not sought at all. That is beside the point. So far as the budget is concerned, I may say to my hon. friend that I am prepared to assume full responsibility for any changes which I may introduce. I would not for one moment try to hide behind Mr. Breadner or anybody else, but I will consult him from time to time as to what effect certain proposed changes in the tariff may have.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
Is that not the work of
the tariff board?

Mr. RHODEiS:	The tariff board will not
be called into conference with respect to the carpentry work of preparing the budget. Certainly we shall have to deal with recommendations that may come from them, but it by no means follows that the minister will not have to have assistance in his office; that will alwas^s be the case.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
Is this not the position,
that the tariff board will make recommendations, but before the government puts them mto effect, they will call in Mr. Breadner and get his advice?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
That is not a necessary
condition at all. Mr. Breadner may or may not be called in on a given occasion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
I happen to have known
Mr. Breadner pretty well for a number of years and it is not necessary for me to pay any particular tribute to his qualifications for the office he held. That he had a knowledge of the tariff and of the work of the customs department greater probably than that of any other man in Canada, is entirely without question. I do not think it is quite fair to criticize him in the way he has been criticized. If he has enforced a law which was perhaps wrongly made by the present government, the government and not Mr. Breadner ought to be held responsible. If he has interpreted the Customs Act and the tariff in such a way as to give offence to the hon. member for Weyburn and some others, they should hold not him but the government responsible. As to his appointment to his present position, I have not a great deal to say, although it is probably quite true that out of the wealth of his experience he can be of material assistance by way of giving advice in the technical effects that any changes in the tariff may bring about.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: That is the situation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
I do not think the government would be doing the right thing if they called Mr. Breadner in now any more than they did before to function in the matter of framing policy with regard to the tariff. When I happened to be in charge of the Department of National Revenue and he was commissioner of customs-and I think he was appointed by the government of which I was then a member-his salary was $10,000 and his superannuation, had he cared to resign, would have been something like $7,000. In the last two years his salary has been $12,000. I question whether the sum given by the minister, I believe quite sincerely, of $2,000 as the differ-

Supply-Finance-Salaries
ence between his superannuation and salary, is correct; I think it would probably be nearer $3,000 or $-1,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: At a later stage in the committee I shall give the exact figure, but I can assure my hon. friend that from memory I am fairly well satisfied it is less than $2,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: I am not in any case particularly quarrelling with that; it is quite possible Mr. Breadner could be worth at least $3,000 or $4,000, to put the situation mildly, in the way of giving advice to the government with regard to tariff matters, what effect a change in one item may have upon others. Those who have had some experience with the customs department know that a very real factor in the situation is that one who is not familiar with tariffs and the way in which 'the department is conducted does not realize how, by making one change, you may upset several schedules and cause a great deal of trouble. Mr. Breadner's advice .in that respect may be very valuable. But I say again that I do not think it should be the duty of an administrator to enunciate and put into force policies. That is the duty of the government and of no one else, and the government should take the responsibility as the minister says he is quite willing to do.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
I strongly protest against the first part of the remarks of the Minister of Finance about Mr. Breadner. The reason is this, that he spoke in the tone of one delivering a funeral oration in regard to a man who is alive, who is only seventy-one years old and who is still very active. I know Mr. Breadner personally and I admit he is a very clever, active man and one always well disposed to give information when he is asked for it. But on the other hand it is most curious that this government is asking for an adviser in financial matters after all changes are made in them. All the changes were made without advice; they were all made in 1930 and the former tariff board was thrown out at that time. The same thing applies to 1931 and 1932. Then we come to 1933 when a tariff board is established after all the changes have been made and the government asks for advice-advice after the milk is spilled. That is the situation. I have nothing to say against Mr. Breadner; I would not offend him; I believe he is a good civil servant who may hold wrong views in certain respects, but his views can be discussed in the house only after they have been accepted by the government and therefore I do not see the necessity of the government having an
adviser in financial matters after all the wrong has been done. If he drafts a treaty, I wonder why he does not draft one between the hon. member for Weyburn and the Minister of Finance.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: Or the tariff board.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: Yes. He would show his skill by drafting such instruments of peace and he could also submit them to the League of Nations. I admit that Mr. Breadner is a very clever man and has rendered good service to the state, but I do not understand why the Minister of Finance and the government should have an adviser in financial matters when they refuse the very sound advice which is offered by all the members of the opposition. Our advice is not so expensive; we give it free and we give it in all candour for the benefit of the government. My point is this: We give them sound advice; it is free to them and they can accept or reject it. They reject it all the time. The hon. member for Weyburn at times gives very sound advice to the government and if the government followed it, Canadian trade would be much better. I understood the Minister of Finance to say that he does not always ask for Mr. Breadner's advice. The minister has a button on his desk. Sometimes he presses it and says "I need Mr. Breadner." Sometimes he does not. But when Mr. Breadner gives his advice, does the minister follow it? If he does not follow it, why? Is he free to accept or reject Mr. Breadner's advice? I believe not. I think, if my hon. friend were free to accept or reject Mr. Breadner's views, this would be much better, but probably, as all of us understand, it is not the views of Mr. Breadner, who knows something, that are imposed upon the government; it is the views of one who knows nothing and decides, with blind eyes and without asking for sound information from anyone, all questions that are submitted to the government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
I understand that while this discussion is taking place, down at the Connaught building a presentation is being made to Mr. Breadner. The words that are being said here and the presentation being made to him there scarcely blend. But I suppose it is the way of the world-sic transit gloria mundi. As to the wisdom of the appointment of Mr. Breadner, opinions may differ. Mr. Breadner has been many years in the service. He is a civil servant and must serve under the law, and if he has made errors in interpretation of the law he has nevertheless given long years of faithful service. This is an-
Supply-Finance-Salaries

other instance where it is fearfully hard for a large proportion of those in the service of the government to reconcile certain attitudes taken and certain situations created in the last year or two by the dismissal of employees, the abolition of positions, by superannuation and by many other means of a similar nature. It is extremely hard for some who have laboured hard for many years, just as industriously as Mr. Breadner has, but who have not reached a standard of salary comparable to Mr. Breadner's and that of a few others yet in the public service, to understand why they should be let out and others taken on at salaries four or five times as great, and this is done under the guise-I do not use the word in any unkind way-of economy. People hardly understand that. When the government wants to practise economy it effects a sort of right-and-left, hit-and-miss decrease in the number of employees; some who might well be retired under superannuation, thus saving by their salaries the present salaries of three or four other clerks, are maintained in their positions. These are just suggestions that I want to place before the minister. If he would kindly let the people understand why these things are done it might alleviate the sentiment of, shall I say, hostility that exists towards the retention in the service of certain employees while others are retired.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: I have no fault to find with the remarks of my hon. friend, and I hope he will not misunderstand me when I say that the question he raises is an age old question. I have no doubt in the world that the section-man labouring on the Canadian National Railways at the lowest wage rate, exposed to all weathers and to hazardous conditions, might find it difficult to understand why he should work for $1,000 a year or less, when the president of the railway who rides by in his private car receives a salary of $75,000 a year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: Or more.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
Or more. But there you
are. My hon. friend may think that Mr. Breadner is worth the sum he is receiving, or he may not; that is a debatable question. The fact is that that is the salary he receives and has received for a number of years. Furthermore I think in fairness to Mr. Breadner I should say that it is not out of line with the salary which he received and which he could have continued to receive had he stayed n private employment. The only point I wish to make which I did not make before is that we are not establishing a position here. When in the natural course of events Mr. Breadner is no longer with us the post ceases.

We are merely trying to make available to the state, at the small sum involved, representing the difference between his superannuation and the salary which is given, his accumulated wisdom and experience which can be of service to the various departments of the government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: Since this government took office certain changes have been made in the customs tariff, which comes under the department of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. Certain changes also have been made in the Customs Act, which comes under the Department of National Revenue. Everyone who has had anything to do with the importation of goods knows that those changes in the customs act have had a more mischievous effect on the trade of the country than even the changes in the tariff. And those changes in the Customs Act were made when the same Mr. Breadner was adviser to the Minister of Customs. After those changes were made and the disastrous effects on our trade were seen, in accordance with promises made at the time of the Ottawa agreements a tariff board was to be set up, and was set up by the government. They chose as chairman of the board a very capable and fair-mindied man, and that man said to the commissioner of customs: "Some of the things you are doing are against the law, the law you yourself have made; and you must stop it." What answer does the government make? They take that same man and put him into an advisory position in a department where he oan pass judgment on the decisions of the tariff board. I think it is a shameful thing to do.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: Hear, hear; that is what has been done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hope that the heat engendered by my hon. friend from Weybum will not unduly affect his system.
I assure him it is quite unwarranted by the circumstances. I am quite prepared to discuss tariff matters and the iniquities of this government when we come to deal with tariff items, as we shall at a later stage.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: This is one of them now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
No, this is not a tariff item.
I can say to my hon. friend that the governments which he has supported and which I have opposed have taken certain action in regard to tariffs to which I have strenuously objected. That may seem strange to him, yet it is so. But I never for one moment thought of attributing the blame for those things to

Supply-Finance-Salaries
one of the officials of the department. May I say to my hon. friend that I would be equally just in blaming Mr. Breadner for the tariff attitude of preceding administrations as he is now in blaming him for any action we may have taken because Mr. Breadner, if I mistake not, was an employee of the government during the whole -time it was headed by -my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition. I know my hon. friend's opinion of this government is not very high-

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: No, it is not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: -but he should realize that we are at least capable of making our own mistakes. I may say to my hon. friend, if it is any comfort to him, -that the mistakes of this government are made by the government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: Decidedly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: We assume full responsibility for them, and do not think it is fair that any official, of whom there are many hundreds serving this country loyally, should be blamed for the decisions of the government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: A question was put a minute ago to the Minister of Finance to which he gave an answer. I should like to repeat the question. It is this: does the inspector general of banks know the hidden reserves of the banks and how they are handled?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
I can only answer as I did before. I have discussed this matter with the inspector general of banks on different occasions and my information is that he has full cognizance of all the reserves of all the banks. I do not think I can make my answer any more complete.
Mr. -COOTE:	Before the item carries, in
regard to the transfer of Mr. Breadner from the Department of Customs to the Department of Finance, I think it is fair to say that the administrative record of the Department of Customs for the last couple of years certainly justifies the retirement of Mr. Breadner. If it is necessary to keep him in the service I think it is far better to have him in the Department of Finance than administering the Department of Customs. To put the matter briefly, I think Mr. Breadner has influenced the tariff policy of Canada long enough, and for my part I should like to see him superannuated.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
I should like to ask the
minister whether under this item we may discuss the salary deduction or reduction in regard to the civil servants?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: There will be ample opportunity to discuss that matter at a later stage. If my hon. friend would do so I would prefer that he defer his discussion, because I may say to him that the matter has not .been discussed as yet.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
I should like to point out
to this committee that if Mr. Breadner was the sinner that he is said to have been, we on this side of the house must share part of that sin. It was the Liberal party that appointed Mr. Breadner, and from the discussion to-day I cannot find that any complaint was made against him during the time he was in charge of the department under the Liberal regime. I think it is unfair, now that he is passing out of the picture, to have criticisms made as to the work which he did. It is quite true, as the Minister of Finance says, that the government is at least capable of making its own mistakes. We all agree with that, but we must never forget that an official is acting under the instructions of the government. The voice is always the voice of Jacob but the hands may be the hands of Esau. In that respect I would say that the hands of Mr. Breadner, under both the Liberal and Conservative regimes always have been the willing hands of Esau.
Let me say, Mr. Chairman, that I have had relations with Mr. Breadner for very many years, and as an administrator I have always found him efficient, and an affable gentleman as well. He was able to establish very pleasant contacts with the public. I do not think any man ever left his presence without feeling that he had been treated in a most gentlemanly way, not that he got by any means what he wanted, but at least he felt t-hat he was getting a square deal and fair play. I think that is the general consensus of opinion, and I would say that Mr. Breadner, with all his experience covering a period of thirty-five or forty years, is worth the couple of thousand dollars he is now receiving from the department and the government. In fact I feel that if the union found that he was getting a mere pittance of $2,000 the government might be brought before the proper tribunal for employing people at what we might call Chinese cheap wages. Either he is worth what he ought to get or he should be retired altogether. For $2,000 you cannot expect a man to give you $12,000 worth of work. I am rather against the principle of employing a man at less than a decent salary; either he is worth $10,000 or $12,000, as the case may be, or he should be retired. I think it may be generally said, however, that everyone will think of Mr. Breadner in the most pleasant
76S

Immigration Act-Mr. Heaps
way. I do not say that I agree with his policies, if they can be called policies, because after all he was merely carrying out the wishes of the administrations which employed him. I think it would have come with better grace from those on this side of the house who have criticized him if they had criticized him also for the period during which he was employed under the Liberal regime.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext: We held him down.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
I do not think we held
him down. Those of us who know Mr. Breadner will admit that he could not be held down; he had strong views to express and he expressed them to all and sundry. During his term of office it is well known that he organized the income tax department as well as the excise department, with everything which that entailed during the wild liquor orgies which were going on across the border during the so called prohibition days, and there was no man who was busier with his duties than Mr. Breadner was. There has not been a word of complaint with regard to Mr. Breadner during the time the Liberal regime employed him, so he could not have become such a terrible person immediately he was taken over by the Conservative administration. Either he is a good man now or he was not a good man then. I do not like to see these distinctions made between parties when it comes to the retirement of an official who has been in the employ of the government for well nigh forty years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
Shall the
item carry?

maintopic: SUPPLY-B.C. SALMON FISHERY STATEMENT OF ME. REID ON MOTION FOR SUPPLY RESPECTING PURSE SEINE FISHING
speechtext:
I was just going to ask the

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO DEPORTATION OF IMMIGRANTS CLASSIFIED AS PUBLIC CHARGES

speechtext:
Mr. A. A. HEAPS (North Winnipeg) moved the second reading of Bill No. 14, to amend the Immigration Act.
He said: I have just a word or two to add to the remarks I made yesterday on the introduction of this bill. As I then stated, the main purpose of this amendment is to make it optional, instead of obligatory as it is at present, for the local authorities to notify the federal government when a person becomes a public charge. The proposed change does not seek to amend in any way the definition of a "public charge." As a result of the unusual conditions and the amount of unemployment prevalent throughout this country there has arisen a situation which I do not think was anticipated at the time the act was drafted. There is a vast number of men at the present time who are compelled to seek public relief, and, who thereby become a public charge absolutely through no fault of their own but mainly because of economic conditions. It appears from what I understand of the situation that many of the municipalities do not seem to be anxious to notify the federal government of such persons who have become a public charge by being in receipt of unemployment relief, but they claim that in view of the present wording of the act they are compelled to notify the federal authorities. I also understand that in most cases in which they have been so notified that persons have become a public charge by the acceptance of unemployment relief, the federal government has taken no action. There is no doubt that great hardship may be inflicted on many of these individuals, many of whom have come to this country in good faith in the hope of obtaining work, but who unfortunately now find themselves in the ranks of the unemployed. Some of them have come here with fairly large sums of money, and now that their own savings have vanished they are compelled to seek assistance from the public authorities, and in many cases the threat has been held over them that if they accept unemployment relief they will be subject to deportation by the federal authorities. I think one of the most cruel things in connection with these cases is that this threat

Immigration Act-Mr. Gordon
of deportation is held over the heads of many persons who are really of excellent character. The change which I am proposing and asking the house to accept would make it optional for the local authorities to notify the federal authorities as to a person becoming a public charge.
I think that this change is desirable for another reason, and that is that our local authorities are the best judges of who should be subject to deportation. They are in a much better position to understand the local situation than the federal authorities at Ottawa, and if the change I am proposing is accepted it would relieve the local authorities of a great deal of the trouble to which they are now put in notifying the federal government, and relieve also the federal government from taking action in the matter. I think that the minister will realize that it is a very reasonable request I am making at this time, and he must also be aware of the vast amount of trouble that is caused by making it obligatory upon the local authority to notify the federal Department of Immigration of these cases. I therefore trust that the minister and the house will accept the amendment I am proposing to section 40 of the Immigration Act.

Hon. IV. A. GORDON (Minister of Immigration) :	Mr. Speaker, this bill seeks to
amend section 40 of the Immigration Act by striking from the section the words "public charge or" in order to remove from the operation of the section those who now are liable to be returned to their country of origin by reason of becoming public charges.
It must be borne in mind that every country in the western world, because those are the countries where migrants in any numbers go, has laws very similar to the laws of this country, bringing within what are called the [DOT]undesirable classes the same sort of persons as are described in section 40 of our Immigration Act. Under that section as it stands at present, when a person who has been in this country less than five years, becomes a public charge, that is, when he has to be kept by his fellow taxpayer, it becomes the duty "of any officer cognizant thereof, and the duty of the clerk, secretary or other official of any municipality in Canada wherein such person 74726-49
may be, to forthwith send a written complaint thereof to the minister, giving full particulars." Then upon the minister receiving the complaint the situation is reviewed, and if it appears in the judgment of the minister that the alien who is here, let us say, on probation, because that is really what it means, is undesirable by reason of his being a public charge, deportation may be ordered. I have some sympathy with the hon. member who sponsors this resolution (Mr. Heaps), perhaps because of the local situation in the city which he represents, but the change that is sought would remove a person who becomes a public charge from the operation of this section, and it would then no longer become the duty, under the statute, of the clerk of the municipality or other officer cognizant of the facts to report the situation to the federal department. It would be left to the discretion of the clerk of the municipality or other official whether to do it or not. In other words, a different sort of law might prevail in every municipality in Canada because I think no one will disagree with me when I say that the clerks of the municipalities throughout Canada are not likely to adopt a uniformity of view. It is left to their discretion, perhaps on the assumption that they are discreet. The exercise of discretion placed in the hands of municipal officials in the various municipalities throughout Canada in a matter of this kind, I greatly fear would take away any possibility of uniform application of the provisions of the Immigration Act.
The hon. member said that the threat of deportation is held over the heads of those who are public charges. That statement has been made before and on a number of occasions I have investigated to see whether it is a fact. My investigations did not reveal that that position has been established.
I appreciate that there may be desirable people from other lands who have not yet acquired Canadian domicile and who may be at present unemployed through misadventure or other causes. It is possible that such people may have to seek relief but I can assure hon. members that if on review of the facts-it is my duty to review the facts in such cases, and I do it-it is found that there is even a possibility of the alien being absorbed into gainful occupation, this section will not be invoked. I recognize the difficulty which certain people have in procuring employment in certain sections and at times I have had our officers endeavour to find employment for those who are unable to take advantage of opportunities which might present themselves to others more active. It is possible that a

Immigration Act-Mr. Neill

clerk of a municipality, exercising the discretion with which he is invested under the terms of this proposed measure, might come to the conclusion that for certain reasons an alien should not be reported. He might even go further and make it known that his particular viewpoint was that none of these people should be reported, not even the malingerers. It must be remembered that the discretion would lie solely in the clerk of the municipality. Even his own council would not be able to advise or point out the direction in which his discretion should go. If it became known that there was a municipality with a clerk of that turn of mind and the clerk in an adjoining municipality was of a different turn of mind, the whole purpose of the act could be defeated by merely moving to the favourable locality.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) has taken the stand he has in connection with this bill, as it means its end. I cannot agree that it would have all the ill effects which he claims it would. The
[Mr. Gordon.!
fact that the reporting of these men is optional would, under ordinary circumstances, suffice. We must remember that men who are on relief are on relief at the expense of the municipality. I have never heard yet of a municipality that was anxious to pay relief. If a clerk in defiance o.f his council insisted upon not reporting these men, the council would have authority to deal with him. It is not as if it were suggested that there should be no reporting, because it would be found that whenever necessary and advisable cases would be reported. But the fact that it is .made compulsory leads to unfair conditions. The minister speaks about the alien and rather plays on that word, and we have the picture of someone perhaps from Jugoslavia. But we must remember that people born in Britain come under the section, and they are alien in the sense that they have not been here five }"ears.
The minister defies anyone to cite an instance of injustice having been done as a result of the act being invoked. I think he used the wrong word; if he had said being enforced, I think he would have been right. His discretion has been admirable, and I have no complaint in that regard. I have in mind a particular case where I myself brought the circumstances to his attention and his officials acted with promptitude and fairness. It is true that he will use his discretion wisely, but the point is that the clerk is compelled to denounce this man, so to speak, and this leads to a great deal- of trouble and anxiety. I have in mind an instance in my own district of a very decent man and his family who were going to be deported because he had received relief to a trivial extent-it did not exceed S20. He had been four and a half years in -Canada and was therefore liable to deportation. He was a mechanic and a good mechanic, and had worked at his trade, but owing to the depression he had lost his job, and he was doing his utmost, as I was able to verify, to make a living somehow. He was not insisting upon working at nothing but his trade, because he was anxious to get a job of any sort; he showed a disposition to take anything, however small the wage, in order to help matters along. There was no dispose tion on the part of the clerk of the council or of his neighbours or of anyone else to have the man- deported; yet according to the law which it is now sought to amend he had to be denounced to the government. He was not familiar with the law; he did not know that if he appealed to the minister he would eventually be dealt with fairly. The result was a great deal of anxiety for him and his

Immigration Act-Mr. Factor
family. There were special circumstances that rendered deportation very harsh and not only the man himself but other people as well were put to a great deal of trouble bringing the real, circumstances to the attention of the minister, whose action then was all that could be desired. There was no suggestion of complaint in that regard, but the fact remains that there was a good deal of unnecessary trouble, inconvenience and anxiety. The danger which the minister seems to apprehend is that habitual loafers and undesirable people generally will not be reported. But as I said at the beginning there is no danger of that, because the people out of whose pockets the money comes to keep such men on relief will see to it that if the clerk does not report the circumstances he will be made to do so. I am simply expressing my regret that the minister takes the view he does. I do not think that the hon. member responsible for the bill before us suggests that there was any harsh dealing on the part of the minister, but it does create a lot of trouble for people when a man is denounced, so to speak, although no one has any wish or desire to deport him.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO DEPORTATION OF IMMIGRANTS CLASSIFIED AS PUBLIC CHARGES
speechtext:
The difficulty about the present act is that the term "public charge" is not defined, and the result is that a newcomer to the country, whether from foreign lands or from the British Isles, if he has not acquired domicile, and receives unemployment relief, is subject to be reported by the officer of the municipality to the Minister of Immigration. Now, no one quarrels with the minister's administration of this law; indeed, I want to commend him for the humane way in which he has administered it. But why should it be incumbent on the clerk or officer of the municipality to report every case in which a man is receiving relief by reason of the present economic conditions, thus burdening the minister with the review of all these cases? The bill suggested by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) relieves the minister of a certain burden. It places the burden on the municipality, which is more thoroughly acquainted with each individual case, to see whether a man who is in receipt of relief is a law-abiding citizen, conscious of his duties and responsibilities; and if his only sin is the receipt of unemployment relief, surely the municipality, the clerk or the officer, is in a better position to judge whether or not he should be reported. It leaves this discretion with the municipality.
74726-49J
In my humble opinion, it is our duty even under present conditions not to decrease the population of the country. On the contrary, I think the time is coming when some constructive policy of immigration will have to be put forward. If we expect ever to carry the tremendous burden of taxation which we have in this country, and to solve the railway problem, we must see that Canada has a greater population than at present. I think that the bill is a move in the right direction. It will not help the malingerer; it will not help the man who runs counter to the laws of the country, but will meet the legitimate case of either the Britisher who has not acquired domicile or the foreigner who under present abnormal conditions is in receipt of unemployment relief, and who will be given an opportunity to be judged by an officer of the municipality, a man thoroughly acquainted with the conditions in the place, and who knows whether the person affected should be reported to the minister. I am really surprised that the government are opposing the bill, and I trust that the matter will receive their very careful consideration.

It seems to me very regrettable that the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Gordon) is apparently determined to keep this law in its present form, for there is not the slightest doubt that it is a harsh piece of legislation. It may be true that the minister is now called upon to undo some of the blunders of an earlier administration. We remember that for a great many years this country spent millions of dollars in inducing immigrants to come here. Millions of people came, and generally the policy of the wide-open door was accepted b3>- our people. Immigrants came in very large numbers from the British Isles and the continent of Europe. Only those of us who have been closely in contact with individual immigrants can form any idea of what it meant even for one family to break up home in the old land, to sever the ties that had bound them to their home for so many years, and to migrate to this country where they thought they would have an opportunity of earning a Irving. Fifteen years ago, even ten years ago, large numbers of them believed that this was the land of hope and that there was every opportunity here for a man at least to earn a livelihood, if not to make a fortune. But times have changed. To-day we have 1,220,000 persons on relief in Canada. We all recognize the seriousness of that situation. This large number includes many who are comparatively newcomers; indeed, the proportion of new-

Immigration Act-Mr. Woodsworth
comers on relief is greater than that of oldtime residents. This is not to be wondered at because the newcomer finds it more difficult to establish himself. In hard times he has not the reserves that the older Canadians have acquired, and so among this huge number of persons on relief are many who have come here in comparatively recent years and who have not been able to establish themselves.
The minister perhaps was not quite fair when he used the term "alien." As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has suggested, that word carries with it certain implications that are not very generally acceptable. It may be that within this group there are some from continental Europe, but I would remind the house that those people came here on our solicitation; they came with our full consent and they ought not now to be treated unfairly when they, together with many others in the country, are suffering. But in addition to those who have come from continental Europe, there are very large numbers of our own flesh and blood who have come from the British Isles; indeed, the larger proportion of those who have been deported have been British bom. It may be true that they ought never to have come to this country, but we asked and permitted them to come. They are here, and now, with the depression, they are suffering and suffering more keenly than the rest of the population.
Last year, in an effort to reach some sort of justice in this situation I introduced a bill. My bill provided for a definition of the term "public charge." It may be all very well that people who have come to this country who are paralytic or insane and in some way have managed to get by the immigration officials ought not to be permitted to become a permanent charge upon our public institutions. In my bill of last year I made an effort to define "public charge" in such a way that those who would come under public assistance merely on account of lack of employment would not be regarded as public charges andJ so would not come under the provisions of this act. My bill was not acceptable to the minister. I know there are difficulties in the way of defining the term "public charge." This year my colleague has sought to obtain some redress, not by defining "public charge," but rather by a little change, what we thought was a very slight one, by which the initial responsibility for action that might lead to deportation would rest with the municipality in which the man resided. Surely the officials of the municipality are in the best position

to know whether a man is likely to become a good citizen; they know the whole of the circumstances connected with his having to receive assistance, and so this bill would provide simply that report would be optional.
Again let me say that the minister was hardly fair when he insisted so much upon the officials of the municipality doing all this, and upon the discretion of the officials. It is really the discretion of the municipality, and when, in the judgment of the municipality itself, it is thought that the man should be carried by the municipality and would ultimately make good, then it is not necessary that he be reported. I would point out to the minister that when the municipality is not satisfied or cannot any longer carry the man, the final decision as to deportation still rests with the minister. But the whole question is this: Is the man likely to make good? The minister, if I caught him aright, has said that nobody is deported simply because he has come on relief. The minister may be of that opinion, but I doubt veiy much if that is in accord with the fact. If I recall aright, only a few weeks ago, from our own city of Winnipeg there was a case where there was a reversal of the opinion of the department with regard to certain people slated for deportation. I think representations were made by the mayor of the city; I know there was a good deal of public indignation as to the law as it exists to-day and both of our daily papers urged very strongly that some changes along the line that we suggest should be made in the law.
If the minister says his general policy is that a man is not to be deported solely on the ground of his receiving relief, the question is: Who is and) how is anyone to determine whether the man can be reabsorbed in our industrial life? Such absorption might be comparatively easy under normal circumstances, but it is not easy to-diay when we have tens of thousands of our young people going out of our schools and universities unable to find a place in our industrial and commercial life. How can anyone say that men now liable to deportation would not under normal circumstances be capable of being absorbed into our industrial life? I can understand, in the case of men having criminal records or being malingerers, it might be a good thing to get rid of them, but there are thousands of others who, if we had normal times, would) become as good citizens as any of us in the house, and under such circumstances it is not fair to deny to those whom we have invited to come here, an opportunity of making good. It is not generous or fair for us as Canadians, as

Immigration Act-Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver)
soon as we get into a jam, to throw back those people who have come to us in all good faith. I hope the minister will see his .way to reconsider his position in the matter.

complete audit.

I notice that the Minister of Public Works has been very modest in preparing his public works estimates in relation to the item of $2,500 for Campbellton. Possibly the minister does not know the town, but it is no small one; it is indeed a large town and besides it is a big shipping point in the maritimes. As a matter of fact last summer I believe more than forty-one ships loaded and cleared from that port with lumber for export. I understand that very strong representations have been made to the department regarding necessary material improvements at the port of Campbellton, because it is the home of one of the largest industries of the maritimes, a subsidiary or branch of the Fraser Pulp company, called Restigouclie Pulp. It is also a shipping point for lumber for not only the northern part of New Brunswick, but also a considerable part of Quebec in the Matapedia valley. It is admitted that for some years repairs have been greatly needed and demanded. The public wharf is absolutely out of order and I am informed by engineers that the paltry sum of $2,500 will be sufficient only to keep together what is left there. I understand the board of trade and all those interested are asking for a larger amount in order to put

that port into proper condition. If their demands are heeded and their plans carried out, I am informed that the estimated cost is between $30,000 and $35,000. Not only would this enable that port to be placed in a first class condition and encourage the traffic which is sadly needed in that part of the country, but it woidd indirectly relieve the unemployment situation in that district, not only through the employment of labour, and those lumbering towns are places where unemployment is prevalent in these days, but through the purchase of the timber required, which can be cut right on the spot, and the steelwork, which can be manufactured about a hundred feet from the wharf, where there are good steel works and where good friends of the government could provide what was needed. It is the government's own friends who are insisting that this work should proceed; all the material necessary for making the repairs can be secured locally.
This work would be in the interests of economy, because last summer difficulties were encountered on account of the bad state of those wharves and their inability to be used as they should have been. This summer there will be great need for the use of that port, because during the winter there has been an increasei in lumbering operations, and While this may not be known generally, 'Campbellton is to-day the centre of lumbering operations on a large scale in the maritimes. Outside Saint John, which is a national port, this is one of the local ports where a great deal of shipping is carried on for export overseas and to the United States. 'With the high rates of rail transportation the reason for these demands for repairs can be readily understood, because lumber exporters and manufacturers in that district cannot at present successfully compete with other exporters centrally located who have a short rail haul. I submit that the cost of not only ordinary repairs but material improvements at the wharf at Cambellton would be a wise expenditure. The unemployment situation in that district would be relieved by the provision of work early in the spring, and also by the manufacture right on the spot of the special dimension lumber that would be required as well as the work for the steel fabricated locally at Campbellton. I hope the minister will take not only my recommendation but the recommendations of the boards of trade and the captains of industry of that district who have made insistent demands for such repairs. Notwithstanding that it may appear as a demand on the treasury in times when economy and retrenchment

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
are being preached, I repeat that it would be practical economy, because it is economy to spend money to preserve what is there and to make the facilities meet the needs of the case.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. STEWART (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext: The representations that have been made by my hon. friend in connection with this wharf are quite in keeping with those made by boards of trade and chambers of commerce in other directions. Unfortunately we have thought that the revenues at this time do not justify the expenditure, although perhaps the business there would justify it if conditions were better. This vote of $2,500 is just to make some repairs to facilitate ferry traffic, and does not in any way touch the larger question which my hon. friend has mentioned. Unemployment relief works, as my hon. friend knows, have been conducted in cooperation with the province and the municipality; these estimates are not framed for the purpose of unemployment relief, although of course any work carried on does help to relieve unemployment. I can only say that in connection with any program of public works that may be determined upon, my hon. friend's representations will be taken into consideration.

This is a very large item. I would like to ask a few questions about it, and I think other members of the opposition will also wish to speak on it. One particular item that interests me is the item concerning the Baie Ste. Catherine wharf improvement, $10,200. I would like the minister to give the details of that work. It is under the heading of essential undertakings. Is it going to be given under contract, or not? I understood last year that the work was to be proceeded with, that an arrangement had been made with Price Brothers whereby
the government would get control of the wharf. Some minor or temporary repairs were made, but it never came to my knowledge that the government had purchased the wharf. Therefore I ask how the government can spend $10,200 on a wharf that is not public property. I do not object to works being done in my county, but I myself when I was on the government side, and also since I have been in the opposition, have tried many times to have the government come to a decision on the matter, but always the stumbling block apparently was that no arrangement had been arrived at or satisfactory conclusion come to with this company.

My hon. friend is quite right; the transfer from Price Brothers has not been completed. As he knows, there is some complication in connection with their financial affairs. It is not proposed to spend this money until the transfer is complete. The money is required to repair the head block, which was damaged by ice in March, 1933, and was repaired temporarily in April, 1933. The only effective way to repair this structure is to straighten the outer end by widening the head block. The traffic involved is the ferry service for passengers and the royal mail.

What repairs were made last year on that wharf? The repairs then made were supposed to be what was necessary under the circumstances; why is this big amount being asked for; especially for a wharf that is not as yet a public wharf?
I have not the particulars, but my official tells me it was simply repairing the flooring of the wharf.
Was there not a staircase or something additional next to the wharf to help the people embark or disembark?
A movable slip.

Was this work done under contract? If not, who was the supervisor, and who did the work?

I should like to direct
the attention of the minister to the fact that a bridge is very badly needed across a river near the town of Empress at the junction of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. The people of that district have had three or four bad crops, and the construction of this bridge and the building of the approaches would provide work for many farmers with their teams and many day labourers as well. This bridge is on a main highway; it would be of great service to tourists and would be of particular help to the' farmers in that district. The river is crossed by a ferry at that 
point, which is very unsatisfactory. This matter has been before the various departments for two or three years, and I should be very glad if the minister could give some indication as to whether such a work could be considered and the steps that should be taken in order to have the department undertake it.
A bridge wholly within a province-

This is between two
provinces.

-or between two provinces is not in the first instance a dominion matter. The only contribution the dominion ever makes is when the two provinces get together and agree as to the necessity for the construction of the bridge. They agree to contribute to the cost; they approach the dominion and in some instances, where the traffic is heavy and circumstances warrant, some contribution is made by the dominion. This is never done on the initiative of the dominion; it must be started by the provinces concerned, who must agree as to the need for the work and as to their contribution to the cost, and in some instances the dominion makes a contribution.
